scenario: [RFCS.23.6]: a `FactExternal` carries no lifetime, so the receiving engine applies its own schema's lifecycle. This holds on both runtimes, through each one's own `assert_external` ([NCBK.10.4]): the `forward_external` step hands the receiver the FactExternal record the sender's publish event carried ([RFCS.23.1]), not a host assert of the slot values. Two senders, two receivers, each receiver declaring `Ref scope ttl 30_s`. `pub_short` declares `Ref scope ttl 5_s` and feeds `hub_alive`; `pub_long` declares `Ref scope ttl 60_s` and feeds `hub_dead`. Each sender asserts a Trig and pumps, so its rule publishes a Ref; a `publish` asserts nothing there ([LTIE.4.3]), so each holds its Trig alone: 1 fact. Each hub receives at t = 0 and pumps. `hub_alive` then advances 30 s less 1 ns and pumps: its Ref is live, 1 fact. `hub_dead` advances exactly 30 s and pumps: its Ref has expired, 0 facts. Each wrong reading fails: a receiver that took the sender's 5 s holds 0 in `hub_alive`; one that took 60 s holds 1 in `hub_dead`; one that applied no TTL to a received fact holds 1 in `hub_dead`. The schema hash a receiver checks leaves lifecycle out ([RFCS.23.3]), so the senders' differing lifetimes do not make it refuse the record. PATH PINNED: libds's `ds_engine_assert_external` (through pyds `Engine.assert_external`, runner.py) and the Mercury runtime's `ds.fact_receive.assert_external` (test_behave.m's `receive_on_tier`), each asserting under the receiving schema's own lifetime.

pub_short.rules_ds:
schema Trig scope logical:
    v: Int key

schema Ref scope ttl 5_s:
    v: Int

rule up:
    Trig t
->
    publish Ref v: t.v

hub_alive.rules_ds:
schema Ref scope ttl 30_s:
    v: Int

pub_long.rules_ds:
schema Trig scope logical:
    v: Int key

schema Ref scope ttl 60_s:
    v: Int

rule up:
    Trig t
->
    publish Ref v: t.v

hub_dead.rules_ds:
schema Ref scope ttl 30_s:
    v: Int
